findings.title: No seed corpus and no final selection step: EVOREFUSE-TEST cannot be regenerated
findings.quote:
for num, line in enumerate(input_data.readlines()):
    one_data = json.loads(line)

    instruction = one_data["prompt"]
    label = one_data["label"]
findings.claim: The released entry point streams a seed file that must contain the keys "prompt" and "label". No released file has those keys (datasets/evo_test.jsonl has only "instruction"; grep over code/ finds no TRIDENT-CORE/XSTEST seed file - see out/check_repo_inventory.csv rows 3-5), and the script stops after writing one record per iteration; Algorithm 1 line 11 ("Return x* <- arg max_{x in X_all} F(x)") and the reduction of 800 optimised seeds to the 582 released instructions are not implemented.
findings.concern: The paper's first contribution - generating EVOREFUSE-TEST (Section 3.4, p. 6) - therefore has no runnable end-to-end implementation: the seed data, the best-of-run selection, the 800 -> 582 filtering and the assembly of the benchmark file are all absent.
findings.resolution: Please release the 800 TRIDENT-CORE seed records (or a fetch script), the per-seed iteration logs, and the script that applies Algorithm 1 line 11 plus safety filtering to obtain the 582 instructions.

findings.title: Response confidence is scored without the instruction, contra Eq. 5 and Table 2's Log-Prob(y|x)
findings.quote:
tokens = tokenizer(generated_text, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, padding=True)
        input_ids = tokens.input_ids.to(device)
        attention_mask = tokens.attention_mask.to(device)

        with torch.no_grad():
            outputs = model(input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask, labels=input_ids)
            loss = outputs.loss

        perplexity = (2 ** loss).item()
        p_y_given_x = math.log(perplexity)
findings.claim: In the fitness function the instruction is used only inside `model.generate` (line 148); the loss that becomes the response-confidence term is computed from a fresh tokenisation of the generated text alone. Running the released `cal_ppl` with mock objects confirms the scoring forward pass sees only the response string (out/check_confidence_scoring.csv). metric/prob.py does the same: `calculate_logprob(model, tokenizer, generated_text, device)` (prob.py:63) never sees the instruction. Equation (5) defines the term as (lambda/T_k) * sum_t log p_theta(y_{k,t} | y_{k,<t}, x, s), and Appendix B.1.6 defines Log-Prob as log p_LLM(y_i | x_i).
findings.concern: The confidence term of the search objective and the Table 2 confidence column measure the unconditional fluency of a response, not its likelihood given the instruction; a response that is generic and fluent is rewarded regardless of whether it answers x.
findings.resolution: Score the response with its conditioning context (prompt ids + response ids, masking the prompt tokens from the loss) in both `cal_ppl` and metric/prob.py, and report whether the released Table 2 numbers change.

findings.title: LongPPL is computed on the instruction, while Table 2 reports LongPPL(y|x)
findings.quote:
encoded = tokenizer(
        instruction,
        return_tensors="pt",
        add_special_tokens=True,
        truncation=False,
    )
    input_ids_cpu = encoded["input_ids"][0].detach().cpu()
findings.claim: `calculate_longppl` takes a string and tokenises it as `instruction`; `process_file` only accepts records with an "instruction" field (line 268) and skips records without one (out/check_repo_inventory.csv row 22). The released LongPPL therefore describes the surprisal of the instruction text, not of the model's response.
findings.concern: Table 2 heads the column "LongPPL(y|x)" and Appendix B.1.7 defines it over the response tokens (LSD(y_i), key tokens T_key of y_i); the reported "3.45% reduction in LongPPL" is thus attributed to a quantity the released script does not compute.
findings.resolution: Confirm which text was scored, and if responses were scored, release that path (the script currently cannot consume a response file).

findings.title: PRR counts a refuse-indicative string anywhere in the answer, not a response prefix
findings.claim: The released matcher tests substring containment of any of the 31 prefixes anywhere in the whole response. Appendix B.1.1 Eq. (7) defines PRR as 1(exists p in P, Prefix(y_i) = p), i.e. equality of the response's leading segment. On a hand-built fixture of two real refusals and five compliant answers, the released predicate returns 0.857 while Eq. (7) returns 0.286 (out/check_prr_prefix.csv; run check_prr_prefix.py).
findings.concern: Compliant answers that merely contain "illegal", "unethical", "I cannot" or "I must" are counted as refusals, which inflates PRR - the primary metric of Tables 1, 3, 8 and 9. Under the Appendix B.5 system prompt the model is told to begin "Sorry, I can't help with that.", so an answer that opens with the mandated phrase and then complies is also counted as a refusal.
findings.resolution: Align the implementation with Eq. (7) (startswith, or a documented judge), re-run the PRR columns, and report the effect on the 85.34%/29.85% claims.
findings.paperRef: Appendix B.1.1 Eq. (7) (p. 19); Section 4 Metrics (p. 7); Appendix B.5 (p. 24)

findings.topic: statistical integrity of the confidence claim
findings.title: The Table 2 'confidence' metric is a length-dependent sum, confounded with refusal rate
findings.quote:
gathered_log_probs = torch.gather(log_probs[:, :-1, :], 2, input_ids[:, 1:].unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1)            

    total_logprob = gathered_log_probs.sum().item()
    avg_logprob = total_logprob / gathered_log_probs.shape[1]
findings.claim: The script computes both a summed log-probability and its per-token average. The paper's Table 2 values (-43.55 for EVOREFUSE-TEST, -72.62 to -103.08 for the baselines) are of a magnitude that is only possible for a sum: at a typical per-token log-probability of -1.5, totals of -43.5 and -103.5 correspond to 29 and 69 tokens (out/check_confidence_scoring.csv). Summed log-probability is therefore approximately proportional to response length, and short answers mechanically score better.
findings.concern: Benchmarks that trigger more refusals produce short stereotyped answers ("Sorry, I can't help with that."), while benchmarks whose answers are long and helpful produce large negative sums; the reported "40.03% higher response confidence" - one of the three abstract claims - may therefore be a length/refusal-rate artefact rather than evidence of confident refusals. Note that the paper's own fitness divides the same quantity by the response length T_k (Eq. 5), while the reported metric does not.
findings.resolution: Report the length-normalised per-token log-probability (already computed as `avg_logprob`) and the mean response length per benchmark, and/or condition the comparison on the refusal subset only.

findings.title: Three derived percentages do not reproduce from the paper's own tables

takeaways.text: The paper's core method cannot be run end-to-end: the seed corpus (prompt/label) is absent, Algorithm 1's best-of-run selection is not implemented, and nothing produces the 582-instruction benchmark from 800 seeds.

The response-confidence term of the fitness and the Table 2 Log-Prob column are computed from the response text alone, not log p(y | x, s) as Eq. (5)/Appendix B.1.6 define (demonstrated by running the released function with mocks).
The headline refusal metric counts a refuse-like string anywhere in an answer instead of matching the response prefix; on a fixture of compliant answers it reports 0.857 where Eq. (7) reports 0.286.
Two of the three diversity columns of Table 2 and the "34.86% greater diversity" claim have no code at all.
The "40.03% higher confidence" claim uses a summed log-probability, which is proportional to response length and therefore favours the refusal-heavy benchmark.
The human safety block of Table 2 and two of the nine Table 1 columns (Gemini-1.5, Claude-3.5) have no released artefact.

fineItems.text: datasets/evo_test.jsonl holds exactly 582 unique instructions, as claimed (check_dataset_overlap.py).
datasets/evo_align.json contains a chosen and rejected response for every record (0 identical pairs), and the rejected answers are refusals - so the DPO data are usable as labelled.

No leakage between the benchmark and the alignment data: 0 exact instruction matches and no pair with token-set Jaccard >= 0.8 (maximum over the 582 x 3,085 pairs is 0.55) - _audit_code/check_dataset_overlap.py, _audit_code/out/check_dataset_overlap.csv.

The evolutionary control flow does implement Algorithm 1's structure: 9 mutators, GPT judge (safe only), top-L, N recombinations, best candidate, Metropolis acceptance with a linear cooling schedule; K = 10, L = 4, N = 2, tau0 = 0.1, beta = 0.005, tau_f = 0.05 all match Appendix A.6 (I = 5 matches Section 5.3; only lambda differs).

findings.title: Baseline update is a zero-mean random step, not +-delta*gradient; the +- multiplier is neutralised
findings.claim: The update is `step_size * gaussian_orthogonal_noise(gradient, sigma)` with `step_size = 0.1` hard-coded (lines 136, 210), and `gaussian_orthogonal_noise` returns `<ort_direction, noise> * ort_direction`: a *unit* direction scaled by a signed Gaussian scalar. `noise` is drawn with the per-dimension standard deviations of the batch embeddings, so the step length is proportional to the embedding scale, not to the algorithms' delta, and it is zero-mean and symmetric, which neutralises the `multiplier = +-1` that is supposed to implement 'same' vs 'opposite'. `orthogonal_tensor(v)` replaces one random coordinate of `v` by minus the sum of the others, so the returned vector sums to zero (it is orthogonal to the all-ones direction, not to the gradient) and that replaced coordinate is of order sqrt(d)*sigma_g and dominates the normalised direction. There is no additive orthogonal noise term. `delta_multiplier` is never read by this script, and `baselines/all.sh:16,46` only runs on `${dataset}-0p1-16-${config}` directories (eta = 0.1), i.e. on experiment inputs that `group_results.py:155` excludes from the paper's own analysis.
findings.concern: The paper's claim that the comparison uses 'the same number of iterations and the same average step size delta in each experiment', and hence that SiMEC/SiMExp are 'significantly more effective than the baselines', is not implemented: measured on the code's own logic (_audit_code/check_baseline_step.py) the step direction is uncorrelated with the gradient (mean cosine -0.03, sd 0.84), 52 % of the steps are negative for direction='same', and, for an illustrative per-dimension embedding sd of 0.3, the mean step length is 0.024 versus a delta of about 3e-4 - i.e. the 'baseline' is a zero-mean random walk whose direction the +- multiplier cannot control.
findings.resolution: Please report the mean and standard deviation of the baseline's per-iteration step length and confirm it matches the mean delta of the SiM runs at eta = 1 and eta = 10; if it does not, please re-run the baseline with a matched, controlled step.
findings.paperRef: p. 8, 'Applying the same number of iterations and the same average step size delta in each experiment...'

takeaways.text: Nothing in the repository turns the baseline runs into Figure 2b.
Default config stores algo as the string 'both', the drivers test for the list ['both']
Baseline loop applies each input's patch set to the whole batch and repeats the step per batch element
Baseline update is a zero-mean random step, not +-delta*gradient; the +- multiplier is neutralised
No trained ViT weights, and the shipped model configs contradict the paper's architectures
Preparation writes experiments_data/ while the runner scripts read experiments_data_alt/

fineItems.text: Paper/supplement arithmetic for Table 1: main Table 1 is exactly the mean over the three patch options of Supp. Table 1's ranking-change column, e.g. CIFAR10 SiMExp eta=10: (29.633 + 2.333 + 24.133)/3 = 18.70 and eta=1: (3.733 + 0.100 + 3.967)/3 = 2.60.

Line 7 of both algorithms (delta = eta/sqrt(cond) vs delta_multiplier / sqrt(max/min)) is consistent with the paper once the epsilon/zero-eigenvalue issue of delta-step-rule is set aside; eta in {1, 10}, K = 1000 iterations and the 3 repetitions of every configuration are exactly as described (prepare_experiment.py:592-593,636).

Feasible-region capping is implemented exactly as printed in Section 3.1 (compute_embedding_boundaries, experiments/experiments_utils.py:386-445) and is the default (theoretical_min_max: True, prepare_experiment.py:603), including the embedding-weight split by sign and the positional-encoding term.

The core geometry code (jacobian, pullback, eigh, g = I on the output space) is a faithful implementation of equations (2)-(4) restricted to per-patch blocks; torch.linalg.eigh on the symmetric pullback and the jac^T G jac product are used correctly.

Catch-up/Pearson statistics in the main text: r = 0.32 and mean p = 0.08 reproduce exactly as the mean over the 20 SiMExp rows of tables/catchup.csv (0.3158 and 0.0706), so that part of the text is traceable.
Released tables match the supplement for Supp. Tables 4 and 5 (catch-up frequencies/delta_k and the embedding-vs-interpretation distances) to the printed precision.

Data are publicly obtainable: data-preprocessing/text_convert.py pulls ucberkeley-dlab/measuring-hate-speech and uclanlp/wino_bias through datasets.load_dataset, and the ViT data come from torchvision.datasets CIFAR10/MNIST (experiments/models/const.py), so no dataset is hidden.

openQuestions.text: Which values of parameters.json (algo, threshold, degrowth) produced the reported runs, and were the SiMExp runs launched separately? As shipped, degrowth defaults to False (vit_exploration.py:239) even though pullback contains a degrowth branch (logics.py:201-210) that the paper never mentions.

How were the main-text computation times (0.126 / 0.050 / 0.300 / 0.310 s, described as "per patch/token and per iteration") obtained? The notebook only averages the time field, which is the cumulative per-batch wall clock at each saved iteration (logics.py:318-422).

How were the pixel/token-difference means 2.219e-3 (SiMEC) and 83.028e-3 (SiMExp) aggregated from tables/pixel_diff.csv (whose row means span 1e-4 to 6.7)? No aggregation in the notebooks reproduces them.

The main text reports 10.9% realignment and 290.65 iterations for the catch-up effect; the released tables/catchup.csv gives 10.2% and 268.8 (r = 0.32 / p = 0.08 do reproduce). Which version of the table is behind the text?

tables/volume_ratio.csv and Supp. Table 6 differ for the same quantities (e.g. WinoBias eta=1: 30.575 vs 37.574). Since nothing is seeded (grep -n seed finds no seeding in train_vit.py, prepare_experiment.py, vit_exploration.py or logics.py), how large is the run-to-run variability of rho_V?

findings.title: Per-dataset/per-horizon hyper-parameters in the scripts are far broader than Appendix D describes
findings.quote:
--train_epochs 30 \
      --patience 5 \
findings.claim: Appendix D states that the learning rate is chosen from {1e-4, 2e-4, 5e-4}, that training runs 'for up to 50 epochs with early stopping ... for 10 consecutive epochs'; the released main scripts instead use per-horizon learning rates of 5e-5, 3e-4, 4e-4 and 1e-3 (Weather: learning_rate=(1e-3 ...) at line 15), 5 to 50 epochs, and patience 5 (20 scripts) or 8 (5 scripts) instead of 10.
findings.concern: The reported numbers depend on a much finer per-dataset/per-horizon tuning than the paper discloses, and no script or log documents how those values were selected, so the described protocol cannot be reproduced from the text and the tuning budget cannot be compared with the baselines'.
findings.resolution: State the actual search space and selection criterion (and on which split it was scored) for lr, epochs and patience, or release the sweep/selection log.

findings.title: Two learnable per-variate/per-step offsets are trained but not described in the paper
findings.quote:
# learnable delta
        self.delta1 = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, self.enc_in, 1, self.seq_len))
        self.delta2 = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, self.enc_in, 1, self.pred_len))
findings.claim: `OLinear` (and every ablation model) adds trainable tensors of shape `(1, N, 1, T)` and `(1, N, 1, τ)` to the transformed input (`model/OLinear.py:105`) and to the transformed output (`model/OLinear.py:118`). They are initialised to zero, are trained end-to-end, and are not part of Eq. 2 or Figure 1 (which describe `Z = (RevIN(X) ⊗ φ_d) Q_i^T` and `Y = LinearDecode(H_L) Q_o` with no additive term).
findings.concern: The architecture the code trains is not the architecture the paper describes: an extra learned additive term per variate and per transformed component (0.004 M parameters for Weather, 0.26 M for the 720-step ECL model) is missing from the method section.
findings.resolution: Add the term to Eq. 2/Figure 1 and report its effect, or confirm it should be removed.

findings.title: Table 11 prints a 6:2:2 split for ETT; Dataset_ETT_* uses 12/4/4 months (~5:1.7:1.7)
findings.claim: The ETT loaders fix the boundaries at rows 8640 / 11520 / 14400 (hourly). Against the 17 420 rows reported in Table 11 this is 49.6 % / 16.5 % / 16.5 %, with 3 020 trailing rows never used — not the 6:2:2 printed in Table 11 (and encoded in the released Q-matrix file names `ETTh1_96_ratio0.6.npy`).
findings.concern: The paper's dataset table does not describe the split the code implements, which matters because the Q matrices for ETT were generated with a 0.6 ratio (see `ett-qmat-ratio-vs-split`).
findings.resolution: State the actual ETT boundaries (12/4/4 months of the 14 400 used rows) in Table 11.

findings.title: Q matrices come from a variance-divided covariance, not the Pearson matrix defined in the paper
findings.quote: "            cov_matrix = cov_matrix / diag_vec  # make sure the diagonal entries are 1\n",
findings.claim: The notebook builds each variate's lagged covariance and divides element (p,q) by `Var(q)` only. The paper (Section 4.2) defines the entry as `Cov(s_p,s_q) / sqrt(Var(s_p)·Var(s_q))`. The matrix is therefore not symmetric (max |C − Cᵀ| = 1.2e-3 for Weather-96, 1.3e-2 for ILI-36), and the following `eigh(Sigma)` (line 91) silently uses only the lower triangle, so `Q` does not exactly diagonalise either matrix. Recomputing with the paper's normalisation changes the basis only slightly: mean |⟨row_i(Q_released), row_i(Q_Pearson)⟩| = 0.99999 (Weather-96) and 0.862 (ILI-36).
findings.concern: The stated guarantee "Cov(Q_iᵀx) = Λ is diagonal" holds for the matrix the paper defines, not for the matrix the code decomposes; on small-variate datasets such as ILI the two bases differ noticeably.
findings.resolution: Use `np.corrcoef` (or divide by `sqrt(outer(dv,dv))`) and symmetrise before `eigh`, then report whether the reported numbers change.

findings.title: Table 4 prints Wavelet1 ILI MSE = 0.116 where the full Table 20 gives 1.116
findings.claim: Every one of the 112 cells of Table 4 matches the corresponding "Avg" row of Table 20 (its full version) to ±0.001 except Wavelet1 ILI MSE, which is printed as 0.116 in Table 4 and 1.116 in Table 20 (per-horizon 0.483 / 0.943 / 1.251 / 1.786 → mean 1.116).
findings.concern: As printed, Table 4 makes the Haar-wavelet variant almost 10× better than OLinear on ILI (0.116 vs 1.094), directly contradicting the accompanying claim that OLinear "consistently outperforms all alternatives".
findings.resolution: Correct Table 4 to 1.116 (Table 20 appears to be right); confirm no other cell was mis-transcribed.

findings.title: Multi-seed runs are aggregated by the minimum test MSE; no std/CI/t-test code exists
findings.claim: `run.py` loops over `args.itr` repetitions, evaluates each on the test set, and keeps the run with the smallest test MSE+MAE; that minimum is what is printed as "global best_mse", written to `best_log.txt` and to `best_results/<model_id>.txt` (`run.py:626-647`). The multi-seed scripts (`scripts/OLinear/robust/*.sh`, e.g. `--itr 7 --fix_seed 0`) use exactly this harness. Grepping the repository finds no `scipy`, no t-test, no confidence-interval and no mean/std-over-runs code (`check_stats_code.py`), so the quantities reported in Tables 13–15 (std over 7 seeds, 99 % CIs, Student's t-test p-values) are not computed anywhere in the repo.
findings.concern: The only aggregation the authors released selects seeds on the test set, which biases the 7-seed spread reported in Tables 13/14 (and the significance test in Table 15) in favour of OLinear.
findings.resolution: Publish the aggregation script behind Tables 13-15/26 and state explicitly whether the reported mean/std were taken over all 7 runs or over the best run(s); if the latter, recompute them over all runs.

--q_mat_file covid_${seq_len}_ratio0.70.npy \
      --q_out_mat_file covid_${pred_len}_ratio0.70.npy \
      --q_channel_file covid_COV_channel_ratio0.70.npy \
      --model_id Covid_OLinear_${seq_len}_${pred_len}_no_var_corr \

findings.concern: A fixed preprocessing artefact that the paper describes as computed on the training set is in fact fitted partly on validation data for COVID-19 S2 (the test block, rows 268-335, is untouched, so the test metric itself is not compromised).
findings.resolution: Regenerate the COVID Q matrices with train_ratio=0.6 (as was done for unemployment, which correctly uses *_ratio0.6.npy) and confirm which ratio produced the Table 3 COVID row.

findings.title: ETT Q matrices are built from 60 % of the series, spilling into the validation block
findings.quote: "train_ratio=0.7  # 0.6 for ETT and PEMS\n",
findings.claim: The notebook slices the series as `data[train_length - int(len*ratio) : train_length]` with `train_length = int(len(data)*train_ratio)`; for ETT the comment (and the released script file names `ETTh1_96_ratio0.6.npy`) set that ratio to 0.6. The ETT loaders, however, end the training block at row 8640 (hourly) / 34 560 (15-min), i.e. 49.6 % of the series. With ratio 0.6 the Q basis is estimated over 10 452 / 41 808 rows, so 1 812 (ETTh) / 7 248 (ETTm) rows of the *validation* block enter the pre-computed basis (`check_ett_qmat_overlap.py`); the test block is not reached.
findings.concern: A "training-only" preprocessing statistic that the paper presents as computed from `X_train` actually absorbs part of the validation split, which is the split used for early stopping; the effect is small but it breaks the stated protocol. (The same 0.6 assumption is why Table 11 misstates the ETT split, see `ett-split-ratio-misreported`.)
findings.resolution: Regenerate the ETT matrices with the loader's actual training boundary (12 months) and report whether Table 2/17 changes.

takeaways.text: 13 of 24 datasets ship neither raw data nor the Q matrices the scripts require
np.Inf (removed in NumPy 2.0) aborts training at the first epoch on a clean install
No code for the plug-in results (Tables 5, 9, 10) behind a headline claim
Table 8's Mamba (and E.Attn.) columns have no runnable configuration
No driver script for the efficiency, weight-export, lookback, less-data, few-shot and sweep analyses
No code computes the Student's t-test p-values of Table 15 (or the CIs of Table 14)

fineItems.text: The OrthoTrans pipeline is faithful and leak-free. All 84 shipped *_ratio*.npy Q matrices (weather, ILI, covid, nasdaq, wiki, unemployment, cars, power, website, SP500, DowJones) are reproduced exactly from the shipped CSVs by the notebook recipe applied to the *first* ratio fraction of each series (max |Δ| ≤ 3e-9 after aligning the ± sign that LAPACK leaves arbitrary for each eigenvector row), while full-series versions differ by up to 0.55 — the fixed transforms were fitted on the training block only, not on test data (_audit_code/check_qmat_all.py).

No test-set model selection. Early stopping uses the validation loss (experiments/exp_forecast.py:542-547); the per-epoch test loss is only printed; and the "best intermediate stage" selection at exp_forecast.py:829-858 is inert because every released model returns a single tensor, so the reported metric is the plain final output.

Eqs. 3–5 are implemented as written. LinearEncoder.forward does A = F.normalize(F.softplus(W), p=1, dim=-1), x + out_proj(A @ v_proj(x)), LayerNorm, then a GELU MLP with a residual (verified by running the model: row sums = 1.000000, all entries positive; _audit_code/check_model_smoke.py).

The released entry point works once np.Inf is fixed. With the one-line fix, run.py trains and evaluates end-to-end on the shipped Weather data (_audit_code/check_pipeline_smoke.py: pass 1 crashes on np.Inf, pass 2 reports final output mse: 0.16554, mae: 0.20430 for pred-96 after a single epoch with d_model=128/L=1, i.e. the same order of magnitude as the paper's fully-trained 0.153/0.190 for that horizon). The only other dependency that failed in my sandbox was openpyxl (needed by the unconditional metrics.xlsx write at experiments/exp_forecast.py:882), and it is already listed in requirements.txt.
Table 1's FLOPs/memory analysis matches the code (NormLin = N²D + 2ND² vs MHSA = 2N²D + 4ND² for a [N×D] token set).

Splits are chronological and match Table 11 for the datasets that can be inspected: Dataset_Custom 7:1:2, Dataset_Custom2/Dataset_PEMS/ETT 6:2:2, and the scaler is always fitted on the train block only.
Table 11's dataset statistics are correct for all 11 shipped CSVs (dimension and total length match exactly: e.g. Weather 21/52696, Wiki 99/730, DowJones 27/6577).

The paper's own arithmetic is internally consistent: the "Avg" rows of Table 2 reproduce from Table 13's per-horizon values (ECL 0.131/0.150/0.165/0.191 → 0.159, Weather → 0.237, Traffic → 0.451, PEMS03 → 0.095), Table 4/Table 20 agree except the Wavelet1 typo, Table 6/Table 4 cross-check with Table 3 (ILI S1 1.094, NASDAQ S1 0.055), the stated percentage gains recompute (5.5%, 10.0%, 5.1%, 10.1%, 6.7%, 10.3%, 12.7%, 8.4%) and 140 tasks = 13 datasets × 4 + 11 × 8.

The README's dataset link is alive (Google Drive iTransformer_datasets.zip, HTTP 200), covering the six standard TSLib datasets, so the raw CSVs for ECL/Traffic/Exchange/Solar/ETT are obtainable — the Q matrices and PEMS/METR-LA data are not.

openQuestions.text: How were the per-dataset/per-horizon learning rates (5e-5…1e-3) selected, on which split, and was any test-set performance used in that decision? No sweep or selection log is in the repo.
For Tables 5, 9 and 10: were the modified forecasters (iTransformer, PatchTST, RLinear, Leddam, Fredformer, Timer) tuned with the same budget as OLinear, and can the modified model files be released?
Was the Table 15 t-test paired across the 7 seeds, one- or two-sided, and were the 12 p-values corrected for multiple comparisons?
Is the OLinear-C variant intended to be reported for all nine datasets of Table 7, or only for Weather (the only dataset whose channel-correlation matrix is shipped)?
Were the PEMS07 Q matrices computed with a different convention (no _ratio suffix) than PEMS03/04/08 — i.e. which files should exist?

Are the Table 13/14 standard deviations computed from the unseeded seven runs of scripts/OLinear/robust/*.sh (which use --fix_seed 0 --itr 7), and is the reported std the spread over seeds or over horizons?
